questions.question_text: A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.006P(250-P)$. Written in the form $kP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{C}\right)$, what are $C$ and $k$?

options.why: Read the coefficient straight off without multiplying it by $250$ to convert to the bracket form.
Swapped the two results, using the growth constant as the capacity.
Swapped the roles of the coefficient and the capacity without converting the form at all.
Missed the factor $P$, so the extinct population $P=0$ was left out.
Used half the carrying capacity, which is where growth is fastest, not where it stops.
Included half the carrying capacity as well; at $P=360$ the rate is a maximum, not zero.
Left the exponent positive, which makes the population fall towards zero instead of rising towards $600$.
Used $\frac{C}{P_{0}}$ instead of $\frac{C-P_{0}}{P_{0}}$ when evaluating the constant.
Used $\frac{C}{P_{0}}$ for the constant and also left the exponent positive.

questions.question_text: A population is modelled by $N=\dfrac{3200}{1+7e^{-0.5t}}$, with $t$ in years. Find $N(8)$, correct to the nearest whole number.

options.why: Gave the carrying capacity, which the model approaches but never reaches at a finite time.
Evaluated the model at $t=0$ instead of $t=8$.
Gave half the carrying capacity, which is where growth is fastest, not the value at $t=8$.

questions.question_text: A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.24P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{5000}\right)$, with $t$ in years. What is the greatest possible value of $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$?

options.why: Used $0.24P$ at $P=2500$ and ignored the bracket, which equals $\frac{1}{2}$ there.
Used $0.24P$ at $P=5000$; at the carrying capacity the bracket is zero, so the rate is zero.
Gave the population at which growth is fastest rather than the rate itself.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dP}{dt}$ is a concave down quadratic in $P$ with roots $0$ and $5000$, so it is greatest at $P=2500$.
$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=0.24\times 2500\times\left(1-\dfrac{2500}{5000}\right)$
$=0.24\times 2500\times 0.5$
$=300$ per year

questions.question_text: A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{1}{8}P\left(1-\dfrac{P}{700}\right)$ with $P(0)=950$. Which statement describes the long-term behaviour of $P$?

options.text: $P$ decreases and approaches $700$ from above, never reaching it at a finite time.
$P$ increases without bound, because the growth constant $\frac{1}{8}$ is positive.
options.why: Reads the sign of $k$ alone; with $P>700$ the bracket is negative, so the rate is negative.

options.text: $P$ decreases to zero, because the population started above the carrying capacity.
options.why: Overshoots the constant solution $P=700$, which a solution curve cannot cross.

options.text: $P$ stays at $950$, because that is the initial population and the model is at equilibrium.
options.why: Treats any initial value as an equilibrium; only $P=0$ and $P=700$ make the rate zero.

questions.solution_text:
$1-\dfrac{950}{700}<0$, so $\dfrac{dP}{dt}<0$ and $P$ decreases.
$P=700$ is a constant solution, so the curve cannot cross it.
$P$ falls towards $700$ from above and approaches it without reaching it.

options.why: A positive exponent makes the denominator grow, so this curve falls from $100$ towards zero.
Used the $P$-intercept as the carrying capacity; this model has asymptote $100$ and starts at $25$.
Used the $P$-intercept as the carrying capacity and also left the exponent positive.

questions.solution_text:
The dashed asymptote gives $C=400$.
The curve rises, so the exponent must be negative.
$P(0)=\dfrac{400}{1+3}$
$=100$
This matches the $P$-intercept, so $P=\dfrac{400}{1+3e^{-0.4t}}$.

questions.question_text: Why is a logistic model usually preferred to $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$ for a population living in a fixed habitat?

options.text: The logistic model has a carrying capacity, so its predicted population levels off instead of increasing without bound.
The logistic model grows faster at every time, which matches the rapid growth of real populations.
options.why: The logistic rate is smaller than the exponential rate once $P$ is an appreciable fraction of $C$; that slowing is the point of the model.

options.text: The exponential model cannot be solved exactly, whereas the logistic model can.
options.why: Both are separable and both have exact solutions, so solvability is not the difference.

options.text: The exponential model always predicts a decreasing population, which is unrealistic for a growing colony.
options.why: $\frac{dP}{dt}=kP$ with $k>0$ predicts growth; the sign of $k$ decides the direction.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP$ makes the rate of increase grow in proportion to $P$, with no upper limit.
In the logistic model the bracket $1-\dfrac{P}{C}$ shrinks the rate as $P$ rises, and the rate reaches zero at $P=C$.
A fixed habitat has limited food and space, so a levelling-off model fits it better.

questions.question_text: A population satisfies $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=kP\left(1-\dfrac{P}{2400}\right)$ with $P(0)=400$ and $P(5)=1200$, where $t$ is in years. Find $P(10)$.

options.why: Assumed the population keeps tripling, using $1200\times 3$, which ignores the carrying capacity.
Assumed the population has reached the carrying capacity, which it approaches but never attains.
Used $e^{-10k}=\frac{1}{10}$, halving the exponent's effect instead of squaring $e^{-5k}$.
